steps: Confirm the fireplace & clearances

Code-complying fireplace only, never a factory-built fireplace. Confirm the opening is at least 29" W x 22" H x 19" D and that clearances A–D and floor protection (16" USA / 18" Canada front, 8" each side) can be met.

Consult the authority having jurisdiction (building or fire department) before installation to see whether a permit is needed. Install in a code-complying fireplace only; installing in a factory-built fireplace voids all warranties.

Minimum opening29" W x 22" H x 19" D
Side wall / mantel / side facing (A / B / C)13.5" / 20" / 10"
Maximum mantel width (D)12"
Hearth front / side extension16" USA, 18" Canada / 8"

Clearances are measured from the door flange. Reduce them only by means approved by the regulatory authority.
Line the chimney

Run a continuous 6" liner from the appliance to the top of the chimney, meeting Class 3 of CAN/ULC-S635 or CAN/ULC-S640 (label: stainless steel, UL 1777); insulated is recommended. Blaze King recommends at least 15 ft from stove top to termination at sea level.
Prepare the masonry chimney

Have it inspected by a certified professional and cleaned: no cracks, loose mortar, deterioration or blockage; flue area no less than 28in². Fasten all vent joints with sheet metal screws and bead furnace cement around the flue collar connection.

Have the masonry chimney inspected by a certified professional to NFPA minimum standards and cleaned before installing. Its inner cross-sectional area should be no less than the appliance flue (28in²).

Masonry or steel, including the damper plate, may be removed from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit a liner, provided this doesn't weaken the fireplace or chimney or reduce protection for combustibles below the National Building Code. If the fireplace is modified, fasten the manufacturer-supplied metal tag where it will be readily visible if the insert is removed.

Note: the certification label says "Do not remove bricks or mortar in masonry fireplace" (p. 4), while p. 10 allows removing masonry or steel from the smoke shelf and damper frame to fit a liner.

Never connect to a chimney serving another appliance (voids the warranty). Keep an effective vapor barrier where the chimney penetrates to the exterior.
Remove the front cast (optional)
As shipped it is front-heavy. Disconnect the 2 rheostat wires, remove the 8 bracket nuts (7/16") and the 2 thermometer nuts (3/8"), then slide the cast assembly out through the open loading door.
Remove the flue collar assembly
From inside the firebox, remove the 2 nuts (9/16") and remove the assembly from the rear. Check that its gasket is fully intact and adhered to the collar base.
Install the thermostat rod

With the front cast reattached, check the fans haven't shifted and the thermostat is fully open (set screw on the stop). Slide the rod in through the left cast side, interlock the machined faces and tighten the set-collar grub screw.

The front cast assembly must be reattached before this step.

  1. Check the fans are in position and haven't shifted in transport.
  2. Set the thermostat fully open, with the set screw against the stop.
  3. Slide the thermostat rod in through the left cast side and align its machined face with the machined face of the rod protruding from the thermostat.
  4. With both rods fully interlocked, tighten the grub screw in the set collar supplied with the rod.
Fully open, the knob should point toward the larger end of the gradient. If it doesn't, reinstall the rod at the proper alignment (Fig. 4).
Route the power cord

Feed the cord out the lower rear corner of either cast side with all wiring tucked above the front-cover flanges; on the right side, zip-tie any excess clear of the fan. Plug into a grounded three-hole receptacle and never route the cord in front of or under the insert.
Install the shroud kit

Fit one required shroud, S.Z2091 (29 1/4") or S.Z2093 (32 1/4"), assembled per its kit, tight to the rear of the front cast and fastened with the 7 screws. The bypass handle bracket can go on either side.
Level the insert

It must sit level and slightly higher than the protruding hearth front: remove the lower cast front (2 bolts, 5/32" wrench), adjust the 4 corner levelling bolts, then refit it. Fill gaps only with non-combustible material; use the 2 supplied metal strips to slide over a rough hearth.
Connect the flue collar & set in place

Attach the liner to the flue collar assembly so it hangs about 2' above the fireplace floor, then reach up through the open bypass and pull it onto the rear of the firebox. Check the gasket seal, tighten the nuts evenly, refit the bypass shield, close the bypass and slide the insert home.

1. Drop the liner down the chimney and attach it securely to the flue collar assembly, so the assembly hangs roughly 2' above the floor of the fireplace.
  2. Open the loading door and remove the bypass shield (7/16" wrench).
  3. Open the bypass door and reach up through the appliance to grab the hanging flue collar assembly.
  4. Pull it down to align the bolts with the through holes in the rear of the firebox, then pull forward. Its underside must slide along the top of the firebox so the gasket seats; feel the contact area, and if there is a gap, realign it.
  5. Fasten it with the hardware from removal, tightening the nuts evenly.
  6. Reinstall the bypass shield and close the bypass door before sliding the insert into its final position.

To remove the insert to inspect the insert and fireplace, do steps 1 to 4 in reverse.

panels.title: Not enough heat
items: Green or wet wood → check with a moisture meter
Not enough fuel → load fully; a full load burns no hotter than the thermostat setting
Chimney or cap screen obstructed → remove the obstruction
Combustor plugged, coated or not functioning → clean, test or replace
Poor draft or gusting downdraft → measure with a manometer; wind-resistant cap
Tightly sealed house → open a window slightly or install an outside air kit
Too much wood on too few coals → let a larger coal bed build up

panels.title: Too much heat
items: Bypass door left open → close it
Thermostat set too high → lower the setting
Door gasket leaking → replace the gasket and/or adjust the door
Excessive chimney draft → measure with a manometer; install a cap
Thermostat not operating properly → Blaze King dealer
Wood too small → use larger pieces

panels.title: Smoke spills when loading
items: Spark arrestor screen on cap plugged → clean to bare metal wire
Chimney too cold → make certain double wall stove pipe is used
Not enough vertical rise → minimum 36" before elbows; two 45s instead of a 90
Chimney not drafting → thermostat highest, bypass open, loading door closed, wait 5-10 minutes

panels.title: Thermometer won't stay active
items: Check with the fans off for 10 minutes first
Improper operation → check thermostat setting and procedure
Chimney or cap obstructed → clean, remove obstructions
Faulty catalytic thermometer → check its calibration
Wet wood, or combustor plugged / not functioning → seasoned wood; clean, test or replace
Bypass door leaking or not closing → clean around it; adjust or replace the gasket

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Build every fire right on the firebricks, never on a grate.

  1. Check that all the bricks are in place.
  2. Turn the thermostat to high. Turn the fan off, if you have one.
  3. Open the bypass, then the loading door.
  4. Put 10 balls of non-glossy paper at the front and crisscross 20 pieces of kindling on top, with air gaps.
  5. Light it, leaving the door cracked open. Don't leave it unattended.
  6. When the kindling is fully burning, add two or three medium logs. Keep the door unlatched until they catch.
  7. Latch the door. When the combustor temperature starts to climb, close the bypass. Don't leave the door open once the wood has caught; it can wear out the combustor early.
  8. When nearly all the wood is burning and the thermometer reads active, open the bypass and door and finish loading, as far back as possible. Latch the door and close the bypass.
  9. Leave it on high until the fire is well established, then turn it down gradually.
Note: the manual says when to turn the fan on in three places: step 7 (p. 20) says to turn it on to high once the door is latched and the bypass closed; step 11 (p. 20) says after the initial warm-up; and p. 16 says to keep it off until the stove reaches normal operating temperatures.
First fires: the paint cures with a strong odor and some smoke. Burn at a low setting for several hours and open a door or window until it clears.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
Check the catalytic thermometer first. If the needle is still in the red active zone, reload as below. If it has dropped into the white zone, follow the lighting steps instead.

  1. Have the next load ready. Turn the thermostat to high and wait a few minutes for the air flow to settle.
  2. Open the bypass and wait a few more minutes.
  3. Crack the loading door open to let room air in. Give it a minute.
  4. Open the door slowly and load. If smoke spills out, close the door a little until the draft picks up.
  5. Latch the door and close the bypass right away.
  6. Leave it on high until the new load is well established, then turn the thermostat down.

On low settings you may see very little flame. That's fine: the needle stays in the active zone while the burn continues. Besides the gauge, a firebox low on fuel or a cooling room also tells you it's time to reload.

Load wood only within the usable loading area the manual shows as a diagram on p. 19. Loading beyond it voids the warranty and is a safety hazard.
Creosote film on the glass after long, very low burns? Run it on high for about 30 minutes to burn most of it off.

heat.title: Setting the heat
heat.html:
The thermostat knob is on the lower left side of the front. At the high setting the insert burns fastest and gives the most heat. Turn the knob counterclockwise for less.

  • Make every change gradually. Turned down too low, too fast, the fire can go out or the combustor can stop working (the thermometer drops into the white zone). If that happens, turn it back up and let the fire recover.
  • Wood only burns at the rate you set, so don't be afraid to fill the firebox.
  • The thermostat is set at the factory. Don't tamper with it; the minimum low burn rate must not be altered.

Mild days (about 55F to 70F)

Run it on high for 30 minutes after lighting or reloading, then turn it down gradually. Keep it high enough that the thermometer stays in the active zone. If it won't, turn it up and wait 15 minutes. Too warm? Burn smaller loads rather than turning it lower.

The fan (if equipped)

About 30 minutes after the fire is established, match the fan to the thermostat: low with low, medium with medium, high with high. When to first switch it on is given more than one way; see "Light a fire."

Turned it down and the combustor temperature went up? That's normal. It can climb for up to several hours.

gauge.title: The bypass door & catalytic thermometer
gauge.html:
Your insert has a catalytic combustor. Working properly, it keeps efficiency up and emissions and creosote down. Two things work with it.

The bypass door

It sits inside the top of the firebox. When it's open, exhaust skips the combustor, which you use while lighting and reloading. To open it, hook the bypass handle on the side of the latch and pull the rod out. To close it, set the handle on the center of the latch and push in.

Never touch the bypass latch with your hand. It can cause serious burns. Always use the handle.

Keep it closed for normal burning. Left open, it causes too much heat and extra creosote.

The catalytic thermometer

This gauge only shows whether the combustor is working. Red is the active zone. White is inactive: the combustor is below 500F and may not burn clean. In normal burning the needle sits steady in the red.

Won't reach the red? Turn the fan off for 10 minutes, then check again. Wet wood, a blocked chimney or cap, or a coated combustor are common causes. If it keeps happening, contact your dealer.

Note: p. 18 puts the gauge in the lower left-hand corner of the surround, while the troubleshooting chart on p. 36 calls it the thermometer "on top of stove."

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural cordwood only. Hardwood and softwood both burn well; denser hardwood burns a little slower and longer.

Is it dry enough?

  • Aim for 20% moisture or lower. Split it, stack it so air reaches every side, keep it covered from rain and snow, and let it season at least 24 months.
  • A moisture meter is the only accurate test. Split three random logs and take readings 2" from each end and in the middle of the split face, pins in line with the grain. Average the readings.
  • Wet or green wood wastes heat and greatly increases creosote.

Never burn

Treated or painted wood, coal, charcoal, colored paper, cardboard, solvents or garbage. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes and/or carbon monoxide, which may result in poisoning. Never burn flammable fluids such as gasoline, naphtha or engine gel.

Never burn wet, green or unseasoned wood. It can cause excessive creosote buildup. If that ignites, it can cause a chimney fire that may become a house fire and cause serious bodily harm.

Never burn salt-water driftwood. It's very corrosive and will deteriorate the structure of your insert, and burning it will void the warranty.

Never use chemicals or fluids such as gasoline-type lantern fuel, kerosene or charcoal lighter fluid to start or freshen up a fire. Doing so may lead to over-firing, resulting in a house fire and serious bodily harm. Burning other fuels will also make the combustor's catalyst inactive.

Go easy on offcuts, pressed wood logs and lots of small, very dry pieces. Used in excess, they can overheat the firebox and cause lasting damage.

glass.title: Keeping the glass clean
glass.html:
Heat keeps the glass clean. After each reload, leave the thermostat on a higher setting for 30 minutes to an hour before you turn it down for an overnight burn.

Cleaning by hand

  1. Wait until the insert and glass are cool. Never clean hot glass.
  2. Use a soft cloth. Don't use abrasive cleaners.
  3. Rinse the glass well with water after any cleaner. Leftover cleaner bakes on and can be very hard to remove.

Glass coats up fast?

Usually the thermostat is too low, or was turned down too far, too fast. Run it at the warmest setting for the first 20-30 minutes after each reload. Wet or pitchy wood and poor draft cause it too.

Don't strike the glass or slam the door, and don't use the insert if the glass or its gasket is broken. The warranty covers thermal breakage only, not glass that's been struck or cleaned with abrasive cleaners.

ash.title: Ashes & routine care
ash.html:
Wait until the fire is out and the insert is cool. Surfaces, including the glass, stay hot long after the fire is out.

Ashes

  • Remove ashes whenever they come within one inch of the door opening. Leave a bed about 1/2" thick; wood burns best on it.
  • Use a metal container with a tight lid. Set it on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, away from anything that burns, and keep it closed until all the cinders have cooled. Put nothing else in it.
  • Never store hot ashes in a garage or basement. They give off carbon monoxide.

Through the season

  • Look at the catalytic combustor at least three times a season. A hot fire is usually the best way to clean it.
  • Paper-test the door gasket: close the door on a dollar bill and pull it out. If you feel no resistance, the door tension needs adjusting.
  • Check the fan for dust, lint and pet dander at the start of each season.
  • At the end of every season, remove all the ash and have the insert cleaned out and inspected.
Thermostat or thermometer problems are a job for a certified installer. Your dealer handles replacements.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
Slow fires make tar and vapors that condense in the cooler chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot. The hotter the fire, the less creosote builds up.

  • Have the chimney and the insert cleaned at least once a year, or as often as needed. A professional chimney sweep is recommended.
  • Inspect the chimney regularly through the heating season, especially in the coldest months, until you know how often it needs cleaning.
  • Before the chimney is swept, open the bypass so soot and creosote fall into the firebox.
  • Dry, seasoned wood and a closed bypass during normal burning help keep creosote down.

Ice in extreme cold

Most of what you see leaving the chimney is water vapor. In extremely cold weather, with some exterior chimneys, it can freeze, block the chimney and put the fire out. Burn on high for 5 to 10 minutes to melt it.

A chimney fire can permanently damage the venting, and that damage isn't covered by the warranty. See "Safety & chimney fires" for what to do.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If a chimney or run-away fire starts

  1. Turn the thermostat knob fully counterclockwise. Make sure the loading door and the bypass door are closed.
  2. Call the fire department.
  3. Check the chimney, attic and roof for anything hot enough to catch fire. If needed, use a fire extinguisher or a garden hose.
  4. Don't use the insert again until you're sure the chimney isn't damaged. Have a certified chimney sweep inspect it.

Usual causes are the wrong fuel or kindling-size pieces, leaving the door or bypass open too long, worn gaskets and creosote buildup. Have a plan everyone in the house understands.

Every day

  • It's hot while it runs. Keep children and pets from touching it, and keep anything that can burn at least 48" from the front.
  • If the insert or chimney glows, it's over-firing.
  • Run it with the door closed. Open it only to add wood.
  • Keep at least one smoke detector and one carbon monoxide monitor in the room, and a fire extinguisher in a central spot everyone knows.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
The Blaze King limited warranty is for the original purchaser and isn't transferable. It covers units bought from an authorized dealer and installed in the U.S. or Canada, starting on your purchase date.

Catalytic combustor6 years
Steel firebox components5 years, parts
Fan assemblies, modular thermostat, door handle steel components2 years, parts and limited labor
All parts and materials, incl. exterior paint1 year, parts and limited labor

The combustor is free for the first 3 years. After that you pay 60%, 70% and 80% of its retail price in years 4, 5 and 6. For parts warranted beyond the first year, you pay 20% of the repair or replacement in year 2, 40% in year 3, 60% in year 4 and 80% in year 5.

Not covered

  • Gaskets and firebrick; normal wear such as paint color change
  • Over-firing (warped plates, burnt-off paint)
  • Glass that's been struck or cleaned with abrasive cleaners
  • Driftwood, treated wood or other fuels the manual doesn't recommend
  • Installation in a factory-built fireplace
  • Minor noise from parts expanding and contracting; it's normal, not a defect
Report a problem to your dealer within 30 days of noticing it, with proof of purchase. Your dealer makes the claim in writing. Page 40 shows the coverage as a check-mark grid.

conflicts.issue: Current rating on the certification label: 0.58 Amps in the English text vs 0,35 A in the French text.
Thermal floor-protection standard: UL1618 Type 2 (p. 8) vs 'UL 1682 type 2' on the certification label (p. 4); the label also specifies a 1/2" layer (R=1.06) that p. 8 doesn't mention.
Combustor part number: 'Combustor OEM part #115-0335' on the certification label (p. 4) vs 'OEM Blaze King part # S.CAT2425' (p. 26) and S.CAT2425 COMBUSTOR ASSEMBLY in the parts list (p. 38).
conflicts.reason: Two numbering systems, not a misprint: 115-0335 is the combustor OEM part number printed on the certification label (p. 4); S.CAT2425 is Blaze King's own part number for the supplied combustor (p. 26), listed as the combustor assembly in the parts list (p. 38). The guide shows both and says what each is.

conflicts.issue: Fan timing at light-up: step 7 says turn fan(s) on to high once the door is latched and the bypass closed; step 11 says turn the fan on after the initial warm up (both p. 20); p. 16 says keep fans off until the stove reaches normal operating temperatures.
Catalytic thermometer location: lower left-hand corner of the surround (p. 18) vs 'on top of stove' in the troubleshooting chart (p. 36).

Masonry removal: the label says 'Do not remove bricks or mortar in masonry fireplace' (p. 4); p. 10 permits removing masonry or steel, including the damper plate, from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit a liner.

Offset allowance: the chimney-height table gives 19 ft for 2 x 45° elbows vs 15 ft with none (0 - 1000 ft), while the same page says two 45° elbows equal one 90° elbow and counts a 90° elbow as 2.0 ft.

review.notes: Figures not transcribed: appliance dimensions with each shroud (p. 7), usable firebox loading area (p. 19), tested low-burn thermostat position (p. 22), Fig. A/B bypass latch positions (p. 18) and the fan wiring diagram (p. 12; some of its labels use the font offset by 29 code points, e.g. ')$1' = 'FAN', decoded only to identify the diagram). Warranty: p. 40 is a check-mark grid (parts / labor / wood columns); the guide uses only the p. 41 and p. 43 text.
